title: Describe him to me
hookLine: Sita sees a monkey in the branches and wonders if she's dreaming, then remembers she hasn't slept
carry: dhyana: see the form you love, detail by detail

lines: A SMALL MONKEY IN THE LEAVES.
cards: Sita hears her own story drifting down from the tree. She looks up into the leaves and sees a small monkey, pale gold, with bright eyes, sitting among the white blossoms.
When something you've wanted for a very long time suddenly happens, the first feeling often isn't joy. It's disbelief. And Valmiki says her first thought is: I must be dreaming.

teach.b: Then she catches herself, and her reasoning is lovely. You can't dream unless you sleep, she thinks, and since Rama was taken from me, I haven't slept. So this is real, or it's my own longing taking shape.
Hanuman climbs down slowly, bows, and joins his palms. Who are you? he asks gently. If you are Sita, the wife of Rama, tell me.
She tells her own story: daughter of Janaka, wife of Rama, taken by Ravana. Then Hanuman says: I am Rama's messenger. But how can she trust a stranger who appears out of a tree in Ravana's garden?
So Sita asks him to describe Rama. Not his name. Him.
And Valmiki gives Hanuman a long, loving portrait: Rama's eyes, his voice, his shoulders, his walk, his steadiness, his kindness.
Detail by detail, Rama comes into the grove, and her joy, still half fear, begins to grow. This is how Hindus pray, too.
Before worship, many recite a dhyana verse, a verse for seeing: it paints the god from head to foot, the color, the face, what each hand holds, so the mind can hold the form before the prayer begins.
Hanuman's portrait works the same way. He doesn't argue Sita into trust. He makes Rama visible, and her heart recognizes him.

how: Hanuman's description of Rama is among the best-loved passages of the Sundara Kanda, and many Hindus begin worship with a dhyana verse that describes the deity's form before the prayer itself.

games.q: your grandmother closes her eyes before puja and murmurs a verse before she offers anything. by today's story, what is she doing?
o: picturing the god's form, detail by detail, like Hanuman describing Rama.
games.why: many Hindus begin with a dhyana verse that paints the deity from head to foot. Hanuman made Rama visible to Sita the same way.

practice: If you pray, picture Rama, or the deity in your home shrine, the way Hanuman described him: start with the face and the eyes, then the shoulders, the hands and what they hold, down to the feet. One detail on each breath.
If you don't pray, picture someone you love who is far away the same way, their voice, their walk, one thing they always do, and notice how close the details bring them.

wordCard.voice: Sita found. Sita realizes she isn't dreaming and tests the stranger by asking him to describe Rama, until Rama is almost there in the grove.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyāna, meditation; a dhyāna verse paints a god's form so the mind can hold it.

carryVoice: Your line: dhyana, see the form you love, detail by detail. Tomorrow, the proof she can hold in her hand. See you then.
